sections.heading: C — Vehicle Equipment, Safety Inspection and Maintenance
sections.markdown:
## C — Vehicle Equipment, Safety Inspection and Maintenance

FACT_ID: sec03-F01 | anchor: A01
Every motor vehicle driven on Hawaii highways must carry equipment that meets established standards, including brakes, steering, a horn, door handles, tires, an exhaust system, lights, glass, windshield wipers, an odometer, a speedometer, bumpers, wheels and lug nuts, fenders, floor pans, a hood with catches and a gas tank [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F02 | anchor: A01
A red light showing to the front, or a blue light visible from outside the vehicle, is prohibited on any vehicle other than an authorized emergency vehicle [A01].
Why it matters: red-to-front and blue are the emergency colors, so private vehicles may not show them.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F03 | anchor: A01
A bell, exhaust whistle or siren is prohibited equipment except on an authorized emergency vehicle [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F04 | anchor: A01
A muffler cut-out or by-pass is illegal, and so is any muffler that makes more noise than the original equipment manufacturer's muffler [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F05 | anchor: A01
Every motor vehicle used on public highways must pass an official periodic motor vehicle inspection, called a PMVI or safety inspection, at least once a year [A01].
Why it matters: the yearly cycle is the baseline; ambulances and new vehicles are the two exceptions.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F06 | anchor: A01
Ambulances must be safety inspected once every six months, while a new vehicle needs no further inspection until two years after its initial inspection on the date it was first sold [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F07 | anchor: A01
Many service stations and garages are authorized to perform safety inspections, issue inspection certificates and affix inspection stickers under the state inspection rules [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F08 | anchor: A01
A Hawaii automobile insurance identification card must be presented to pass the safety inspection, and once the vehicle is approved a sticker is affixed and an inspection certificate is issued that must stay in the vehicle [A01].
Why it matters: no insurance card means no inspection sticker, and the certificate rides in the car.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F09 | anchor: A01
The results of a safety inspection are sent electronically to the motor vehicle registration file [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec03-F10 | anchor: A02
Even if someone else owns the vehicle, the driver is responsible for its condition, and routine care should be carried out regularly by the driver or by an experienced mechanic [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F11 | anchor: A02
A common brake test is to apply the brakes rather hard at four to eight miles per hour in a place where others are not forced to brake too, and the vehicle should not pull to either side [A02].
Why it matters: pulling to one side during the brake test signals a brake problem.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F12 | anchor: A02
If your vehicle has antilock brakes, try them in an open area such as a deserted parking lot so you know what to expect, remembering that they usually activate only above ten miles per hour, activate more easily on a wet slippery surface, and must not be pumped [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F13 | anchor: A02
Brake lamps warn other drivers that you are slowing or stopping, so check often that they light when the brakes are applied [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F14 | anchor: A02
Directional signals let you communicate with other drivers, a change in the dash light indication means they are not working properly, and if they fail you must use hand signals until they are repaired [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F15 | anchor: A02
Door latches and locks provide safety and security, so make sure every door latches and locks properly [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F16 | anchor: A02
The exhaust system carries gases to an exit point that limits fumes entering the passenger compartment and keeps noise acceptable, so keep it free of leaks to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning and replace defective parts immediately [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F17 | anchor: A02
Head lamps are critical for night driving, rain, fog and tunnels, and they must work properly and be correctly adjusted at all times [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F18 | anchor: A02
A front-opening hood has a primary latch and a secondary catch, and both must work so the hood cannot fly open and block your vision while driving [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F19 | anchor: A02
Every vehicle must have a horn in good working condition to give an audible warning, and rear-view mirrors must be clean, firmly attached and adjusted for the widest view of the rear horizon [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec03-F20 | anchor: A03
Safety belts keep you from being injured and can save your life, and Hawaii law requires every front and back seat occupant to use a seat belt [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F21 | anchor: A03
A child under age four must ride in a child restraint, and a child under age eight must be belted in a booster seat if the child is shorter than four feet and weighs less than forty pounds [A03].
Why it matters: the booster rule has two measurements, height and weight, and both the age and the size limits are printed on this page.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F22 | anchor: A03
Air bags are supplemental protection for a first impact only, because they deflate immediately and occupants must rely on belts in any later impact, and deployed air bags should be replaced to keep full protection [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F23 | anchor: A03
The steering wheel should turn smoothly from full right to full left and back, with no more than two inches of free play with power steering, checked with the engine running, or three inches without power steering [A03].
Why it matters: the two-inch and three-inch free-play limits are a classic numeric test item.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F24 | anchor: A03
A healthy vehicle responds quickly to small steering movements, does not pull to either side, and its wheels do not shimmy [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F25 | anchor: A03
Tail lamps and side marker lamps warn other drivers of your presence, so check them periodically for proper operation [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F26 | anchor: A03
Check your tires at least once a month, using the door jamb label for the manufacturer's recommended pressure and tire size, because proper pressure extends tire life and improves handling [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F27 | anchor: A03
Replace any tire with less than one sixteenth of an inch of tread, and an easy check is a Lincoln penny placed upside down in the tread, because if the top of Lincoln's head is visible the tire must be replaced [A03].
Why it matters: the penny test is the memorable form of the one-sixteenth-inch rule.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F28 | anchor: A03
Also check tires, including the spare, for cuts, bulges, tread separation and uneven wear, and treat a slight steering wheel vibration or an unusual noise as a possible tire problem [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec03-F29 | anchor: A03
The windshield must be free of cracks and breaks that interfere with vision, the wipers should clean it evenly without streaks, and the washer reservoir should be kept filled and checked often [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0020]

Misconceptions: the yearly safety inspection is the rule, but ambulances are inspected every six months and a new vehicle waits two years after its first inspection; air bags protect in the first impact only, so belts are still required; the steering free-play limit is two inches with power steering and three inches without, not the same for both; a booster seat is for a child under eight who is also under four feet and under forty pounds, not for every child under eight regardless of size.

Mnemonics: Once a year for cars, twice a year for ambulances, two years free for new; four under four in a restraint, under eight on a booster when small; two inches of play with power, three without; a penny upside down tells you when the tread is gone.

Glossary: periodic motor vehicle inspection, or PMVI (Hawaii's yearly safety inspection); muffler cut-out (a device that routes exhaust around the muffler); antilock brakes (a system that prevents wheel lock-up and must not be pumped); free play (steering wheel movement before the wheels respond); booster seat (a belt-positioning seat for a child too small for the adult belt).

Dynamic facts: the inspection web address and the national highway safety web addresses printed on these pages can change and are not stated as stable knowledge; the intervals, measurements and prohibited equipment are stable rules of this printing.

corpus_stability.reason: The Hawaii Driver's Manual is a periodically reprinted reference (imprint HMG 5/2023, copyright line through 2023); the required and prohibited vehicle equipment, the periodic safety inspection, and the condition and maintenance checks for brakes, lamps, signals, exhaust, steering, tires, belts and windshields rules on pages 18–20 are statutory and procedural content that changes less than once a year, so no BlockedProbe.
